title: Cells: The Basic Units of Life
seo_title: SSS 1 Biology: Cells: The Basic Units of Life Worksheets (WAEC/NECO)
standard_code: SSS 1 Biology: Cells: The Basic Units of Life
standard_text: The cell theory; the microscope and magnification; the structure and functions of the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, vacuole and cell wall; differences between plant and animal cells; movement of substances by diffusion, osmosis and active transport. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 1; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 1 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, organelles and their functions, microscopes and magnification, plant and animal cells and movement across membranes. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: All living things are made of cells.
key_sub: Osmosis is the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane.
body_html:
How to think about it

The cell theory states that all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells. Organelles have special functions: the nucleus controls the cell, mitochondria carry out respiration, ribosomes make proteins, and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; animal cells do not. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration; osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane; active transport uses energy to move substances against a concentration gradient.

Example

Which organelle releases energy from food?

The powerhouse of the cell

Answer: the mitochondrion

Example

Image 20 mm, real size 0.02 mm. Magnification?

image ÷ actual

Answer: × 1,000

Common mistakes

  • Thinking animal cells have cell walls.
  • Thinking osmosis is the movement of salt.
  • Measuring the image and real size in different units.

faq.q: Why do plant cells not burst in pure water?
faq.a: The strong cell wall stops them from swelling too much.

faq.q: What does a light microscope show that the eye cannot?
faq.a: Cells and some organelles, such as the nucleus, magnified up to about 1,000 times.

items.q: Why must cells stay small?
c: as a cell grows, its surface area to volume ratio falls, so exchange becomes too slow
items.e: Volume grows faster than surface area.

items.q: What is the main function of smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
c: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: making lipids and steroid hormones.

items.q: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
c: sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
items.e: The centromeres divide.

items.q: Which factor increases the rate of diffusion?
items.e: Fick's law: rate ∝ area × difference ÷ thickness.

items.q: Why is a virus not considered a living cell?
c: it has no cytoplasm or ribosomes and can only replicate inside a host cell
items.e: Viruses are acellular.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia?
items.e: Centrioles: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia.

items.q: What is the evidence that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
c: they have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and a double membrane
they are found in every prokaryote
they are bigger than the nucleus
items.e: This is the endosymbiotic theory.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of protein synthesis?
items.e: Ribosomes: the site of protein synthesis.

items.q: What is the main function of leucoplasts?
c: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid
items.e: Leucoplasts: storing starch, oils and proteins.

items.q: A nucleus is 8.00 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×1,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 8,000 µm = 8.00 mm.

items.q: How does sodium–glucose co-transport absorb glucose in the ileum?
c: Na⁺ diffuses into the cell down its gradient, carrying glucose with it
glucose is pumped out by ATP
items.e: The gradient is set up by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

items.q: Which structure is found in prokaryotic cells but not eukaryotic cells?
items.e: Prokaryotes also have 70S ribosomes.

items.q: What is resolution?
c: how much bigger the image is
the ability to distinguish two points that are close together
items.e: Magnification without resolution gives a blurred image.

items.q: What happens in metaphase of mitosis?
c: chromosomes line up at the equator, attached to spindle fibres
items.e: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres.

items.q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What happens?
c: water leaves and the cell becomes plasmolysed
the cell takes in salt by osmosis
water enters and the cell bursts
items.e: The membrane pulls away from the cell wall.

items.q: In ultracentrifugation, which organelle forms the first pellet?
items.e: The heaviest organelles settle at the lowest speed.

items.q: What is osmosis?
c: movement of any particle from high to low concentration
net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution
movement of salt across a membrane
items.e: Water moves towards the higher solute concentration.

items.q: What is diffusion?
c: movement of large particles in vesicles
movement against a concentration gradient using ATP
net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
items.e: Diffusion is passive.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)?
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: What is active transport?
c: movement down a gradient with no energy
movement against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP
items.e: Root hair cells take up mineral ions this way.

items.q: Who explained that all cells arise from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula-e cellula)?
items.e: This completed the cell theory.

items.q: Which organelles contain their own DNA and ribosomes?
items.e: They are semi-autonomous.

items.q: Which organelles are called suicidal bags?
items.e: Their enzymes can digest the cell itself.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making lipids and steroid hormones?
items.e: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: making lipids and steroid hormones.

items.q: What is the main function of vacuole?
c: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid
the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Vacuole: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid.

items.q: What is the main function of nucleolus?
c: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids
items.e: Nucleolus: making ribosomal RNA.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
c: a lipid bilayer in which proteins float, with the lipid able to move sideways
items.e: Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).

items.q: What is the folded inner membrane of mitochondria called?
items.e: They increase the surface area.

items.q: Who first saw and described a living cell?
items.e: Hooke saw dead cork cells.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid?
items.e: Vacuole: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid.

items.q: A chloroplast is 5.00 µm long. Its image is 100 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
items.e: Change mm to µm: 100,000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×20,000.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for giving colour to fruits and flowers?
items.e: Chromoplasts: giving colour to fruits and flowers.

items.q: In a photograph a chloroplast is 20.0 mm long. The magnification is ×5,000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 20.0 mm ÷ 5,000 = 0.00400 mm = 4.00 µm.

items.q: Which bacterial structure helps attach to surfaces and other cells?
items.e: Flagella are for movement.

items.e: Rough endoplasmic reticulum: making and secreting proteins.

items.q: What are the stacks of thylakoids in a chloroplast called?
items.e: The fluid around them is the stroma.

items.q: What is the main function of mitochondria?
c: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: What is the shape of the cilia and flagella axoneme in cross-section?
items.e: Nine outer doublets and two central singlets.

items.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
items.e: Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP.

items.q: Which cells contain chloroplasts?
c: some eukaryotic cells only (plants and algae)
items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

items.q: Why is cancer linked to uncontrolled mitosis?
c: mutations in genes that control the cell cycle
items.e: Tumours form from rapidly dividing cells.

items.q: Nonso is labelling a cell model. What is the main job of the mitochondria?

A jelly-like fluid that holds the other parts
A stiff outer layer that supports and protects a plant cell

items.q: Why can oxygen diffuse straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Ions need channel proteins.

items.e: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is a loop, with extra plasmids.

A jelly-like fluid that holds the other parts
Controls the cell's activities and holds the genetic information (DNA)
Controls what enters and leaves the cell
items.e: The cytoplasm a jelly-like fluid that holds the other parts.

items.q: What is the function of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −1000 kPa and the salt solution has −250 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from the salt solution to an onion cell
from an onion cell to the salt solution
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Which statement compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells correctly?
c: only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
items.e: Both have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −600 kPa and the salt solution has −1200 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from an onion cell to the salt solution
from the salt solution to an onion cell
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: A root hair cell has a water potential of −1000 kPa and the soil water has −1200 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from the soil water to a root hair cell
from a root hair cell to the soil water
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −800 kPa and the salt solution has −400 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−400 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer in water?
c: their phosphate heads are hydrophilic and their fatty acid tails are hydrophobic
items.e: Tails face inwards away from water.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Glucose and ions often need protein channels.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model?
c: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that can move within it

items.e: Proteins float in a fluid bilayer.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −200 kPa and the salt solution has −800 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−200 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Which process moves large particles out of a cell in vesicles?
